- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. # Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

# About Half a Billion Dollars of MLB Salary Went to UCL Rehab, 2004 to 2014

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally reports a league-wide study, "under review" at the time of the talk, using public MLB data (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Window:** 2004 to 2014, chosen so that players who had surgery in 2014 had time to return (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Counts:** about 200 surgeries, and on average 180 days of MLB-calendar time missed (z_6M5r7031A [12:14]). About half the players were starters and half relievers, with a small proportion of closers (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Total:** adjusted to 2017 levels, "half a billion dollars" of salary lost over the period to rehab alone (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Excluded:** medical, travel and rehab costs; downtime before the surgery; lost team wins; trade value; and every minor league player (z_6M5r7031A [12:44] to [13:44]). He speculates the full cost might be 1 billion or 1.5 billion and says "I don't know" (z_6M5r7031A [13:44]).
- **Per player:** medical cost of about $50,000, which he calls conservative (z_6M5r7031A [11:13]). (Untested: bare assertion, no method given.)
- **Salary per WAR:** it "balloons" after surgery and does not return to the pre-surgery level until 3 years after the pitcher returns (z_6M5r7031A [10:43]). In Q&A he calls the salary-over-WAR calculation "relatively back of the envelope" and not adjusted (z_6M5r7031A [28:27]). (Untested: back-of-envelope, unadjusted.)

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism; this is an accounting of public salary data. Inference: it counts only direct salary during rehab, which is why the number is a floor on the speaker's own account.

**When to apply** — As an example of costing an injury type from public records by counting time missed and attaching a value. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a Baylor version would count games and practices missed by injury type and position group with Athletic Medicine, with no salary figure.

**When NOT to apply** — The study was under review, not published, at the time. Baylor athletes have no player salaries, so dollar figures and dollars per WAR do not transfer to college. The salary-per-WAR calculation is unadjusted and the speaker's own words are "back of the envelope." The 180-day figure is MLB calendar time. It is professional baseball pitchers only, and it counts surgeries, not all injuries.

**Example** — The speaker's own: about 200 surgeries over 2004 to 2014 and 180 MLB-calendar days missed on average, summing to half a billion 2017 dollars (z_6M5r7031A [12:14] to [12:44]).

**Related** — [[claim--ucl-reconstruction-return-outcomes-mlb-pitchers]] (the cohort data that goes with these costs).

from being invented.
You see, the throwing motion in
baseball, in particular, is one of the
most dynamic motions in all of modern
sports, and it relies on a series of
ligaments and other structures in the
body, especially the shoulder and the
elbow, to allow for stability to throw
at such high velocities and accuracy.
In particular, one of the most important
of those ligaments is the ulnar

[01:36]
collateral ligament of the elbow, and it
runs on the inside part of the elbow,
and it's the main stabilizing ligament
of the throwing motion.
Without it, pitchers cannot pitch with
accuracy or with velocity.
So, what happens when this ligament is
injured?
If you're lucky, it's a small tear or a
a low-grade tear, and a period of rest,
physical therapy, and maybe some
injections can get you along without
needing any surgery.
But for many others who have a complete
tear of that ligament or a high-grade

[02:07]
injury,
they can't get back without a surgery.
And unfortunately, the ligament cannot
just be sewn back together. It actually
has to be reconstructed or replaced with
a tendon from the player's arm,
leg, or even a cadaver source. And we
put that ligament through the bones in
bone tunnels, and this is what we call a
UCL reconstruction procedure.
Now, many of you, of course, know this
surgery by a very different name, and it
was named after the first player to ever
undergo this procedure.
In 1974,

[02:38]
the legendary late Dr. Frank Jobe
diagnosed Tommy John with a deficiency
of his ulnar collateral ligament.
At that time, it was a career ender, and
this may have been what was going on
with Sandy Koufax a few years prior.
But Tommy John desperately wanted to go
back to playing, and so he told Dr.
Jobe,
"Make this better." And Dr. Jobe told
him, "Well, there is no treatment for
this, but I could give you a new
ligament, and I have no idea how it's
going to work. It could make you worse.
You could have nerve damage, and you may

[03:09]
not get back to playing."
And Tommy John said, "Sure, sign me up."
So, he did the surgery,
and 2 years later, Tommy John got back
to pitching, and he actually had a very
long career afterwards.
Since then, however, Major League
Baseball has seen a rash of Tommy John
surgeries.
And this is a typically This is
basically an overuse injury of the
elbow. And we're seeing the numbers of
pitchers undergoing the surgery rise
year by year by year.
In fact, there's been 900 professional

[03:39]
pitchers and counting who have undergone
the surgery.
25% of all Major League Baseball
pitchers playing today have undergone
Tommy John surgery. So, it is very safe
to say that Dr. Frank Jobe literally
saved the game of baseball as we know
it.
The big question is, from a clinical
perspective, why are we still seeing
these injuries? We're really good at
preventing injuries when we know about
them, and we know a lot about Tommy John
injuries, but we can't curb them.
And I think there are basically two main
reasons why we are continuing to see

[04:09]
this injury, and it's not going
anywhere.
The first is that pitchers are throwing
harder than they've ever thrown before.
The average fastball velocity is
climbing up year after year after year.
And what we're doing now is that we're
studying what the impact of that
velocity is on stress at the elbow. Our
group at Henry Ford is actually using
new wearable technology that detects
elbow stress and elbow torque at the
medial elbow, right where the UCL is,
and we're trying to figure out what the
link is between velocity and elbow
stress.

[04:39]
And what we found in study after study
using this technology is that the faster
you throw,
the more stress there is at the elbow.
And this is not arm speed, this is pitch
speed. And it used to be that we would
tell our kids, "Don't throw curveballs
or change-ups. Don't throw off-speed
pitches. That's too much stress at the
elbow. Just stick with straight
fastballs."
Well, what we're finding is, whether
you're a 12-year-old youth pitcher or a
professional pitcher,
those fastballs that have high velocity
impart greater stress to the elbow. And

[05:10]
this has been borne out in numerous
different studies of independent studies
from our group.
We wanted to take it one step further.
Maybe fatigue is playing into this, cuz
this is an overuse injury. And so, we
did a study recently where we took a
bunch of pitchers, and we put them
through a simulated game, a seven-inning
game. And after each inning, we said,
"How tired are you on a score of 1 to
10?"
And naturally, that score went up inning
by inning, which is not surprising.
What we found also was that the peak
fastball velocity around inning five

[05:40]
started to dip. Again, that in of itself
is not that surprising.
What we were surprised to see was that
when that stress should have come down,
it actually went up. So, unlike the
pitchers that we tested that were not
fatigued,
the velocity-stress relationship totally
broke down in our fatigued players. And
this is a real link to how we can
decipher the the connection between
fatigue, velocity, and elbow stress.
The second reason why we're not seeing
any drop in Tommy John surgeries at the

[06:10]
professional level has nothing to do
with professional sports. It's actually
far more sinister.
One of my colleagues sent me this
picture of his kid and his Little League
team.
And it doesn't take a doctor to know
that kids of this age should not be
using ice bags to ice down their elbows
after playing.
It used to be back in the day that
baseball players would play baseball in
the spring, but then they'd play
football in the fall, and basketball in
the winter. And we talked about this
actually at the the Gladwell-Epstein

[06:40]
uh discussion just an hour ago.
But now,
people are playing sports at an earlier
age year-round. So, for the baseball
players who are obviously using the
muscles of their shoulder and elbow,
they're not getting that rest. They're
playing fall ball, winter ball, spring
ball, summer ball, weekend ball, high
school ball, travel ball,
and they're pitching year-round. I give
talks to a lot of facilities and
leagues, junior leagues, 12-year-olds,
14-year-olds, and their parents, and
these kids are playing non-stop. In

[07:10]
fact, there's a foot of snow in
Michigan, there's snow right now, and
there are kids all over the area playing
in indoor facilities when they should be
doing something else. And what happens
is this single sport specialization at
an early age, before kids are skeletally
mature, is causing a burnout of their
muscles and their tendons.
We did a study where we took 200 healthy
youth baseball players. These are kids
that are playing. They're not
complaining of pain. And we did a survey
with them when I was in residency in New
York City.
What we found is that 75% of players
admitted to having arm pain.

[07:41]
25% of the kids had symptoms that were
suggestive of a legitimate overuse
injury. And this was the worst part. 50%
of players

=== claim--faster-pitches-load-the-elbow-more
---

# Faster Pitches Put More Stress on the Elbow, Youth and Professional

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally's group at Henry Ford uses a wearable sleeve that detects stress and torque at the medial elbow, "right where the UCL is" (z_6M5r7031A [04:09]). The speaker reports that, "study after study," the faster the pitch, the more elbow stress, and that this is pitch speed, not arm speed (z_6M5r7031A [04:39]). The speaker says it holds for a 12-year-old youth pitcher and for a professional, and that it has been borne out in "numerous" independent studies from his group (z_6M5r7031A [04:39] to [05:10]). The speaker contrasts it with older advice to avoid curveballs and off-speed pitches and "stick with straight fastballs" (z_6M5r7031A [04:39]).

Related statements from the talk:
- Arm slot: studies of slot and release point exist, and "so far" slot has not shown increased elbow stress; this is the group's next stage (z_6M5r7031A [22:33]).
- Device limit: the sleeve relies on a throwing motion, so it cannot measure elbow stress in hitters (z_6M5r7031A [21:23]).
- Trend: average fastball velocity is climbing year over year, which the speaker offers as one of two reasons the injury persists (z_6M5r7031A [04:09]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism. Inference: a faster release plausibly needs more force through the arm, so more load at the elbow is plausible, but the talk does not say so.

**When to apply** — As background when a throwing sport (baseball, softball) asks whether to monitor throwing stress or velocity. Eric's baseline: a test or technology that "doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need" has no place (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q3). Inference: ask first what decision a sleeve or velocity number would change, then check validation (the talk does not describe any validation of the sleeve).

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the talk names no study design, effect size, sample size or range for these studies, only the speaker's summary of "study after study". The studies are the speaker's group's own, summarized aloud. The sleeve's validity is not discussed in the talk. It covers pitching only; the speaker says UCL injury is essentially one position of one sport (z_6M5r7031A [21:54]). The slot finding is a preliminary "so far." Do not use it as a velocity limit for any athlete.

**Example** — The speaker's own contrast: the old coaching rule was to avoid curveballs and change-ups because of elbow stress, while the speaker's group finds high-velocity fastballs also impart greater stress, in a 12-year-old and in a professional (z_6M5r7031A [04:39] to [05:10]).

**Related** — [[claim--fatigue-breaks-the-velocity-elbow-stress-link]] (the same sleeve under fatigue). [[claim--youth-specialization-survey-and-early-surgery]] (the second cause the speaker gives for the injury).
=== claim--fatigue-breaks-the-velocity-elbow-stress-link
---

# In Fatigued Pitchers the Velocity-Stress Link Broke Down

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally's group put pitchers through a simulated seven-inning game and asked for a fatigue rating from 1 to 10 after each inning (z_6M5r7031A [05:10]). The ratings rose inning by inning. Peak fastball velocity began to dip around inning five, "not that surprising" to him (z_6M5r7031A [05:10] to [05:40]). What surprised the group: when elbow stress should have come down with the lower velocity, it went up. Compared with pitchers who were not fatigued, "the velocity-stress relationship totally broke down" in fatigued pitchers (z_6M5r7031A [05:40]). The sample size is not stated, and the talk says the study was done "recently."

His hypothesis, offered in Q&A: throwing starts from the toes, back and core, and as those muscles fatigue while the pitcher tries to hold velocity, "the arm's doing everything" (z_6M5r7031A [24:11]). For a 13-year-old's parents he suggests core and bodyweight exercises such as planks, not heavy lifting, and says his group will start looking into this (z_6M5r7031A [24:11] to [24:42]).

**Why it works** — The kinetic-chain account above is the speaker's hypothesis, not a tested result. He illustrates it with his own tennis serve (z_6M5r7031A [23:40] to [24:11]). The simulated-game study did not measure the other body segments in anything the talk reports.

**When to apply** — As a prompt to check whether an output (velocity, jump height, sprint speed) still holds while a driver or strategy metric changes late in a session or week. Eric's baseline: force-plate reporting picks output, driver and strategy metrics (adopted from Hawkin Dynamics, not Eric's own framework; hd-odsf-metrics.md). Inference: this finding is an example of output alone misleading, since the velocity looked acceptable while the stress rose. Eric's baseline: bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk and comes before loaded work (Inferred, HHPR 5355 course team position, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: this matches the speaker's planks-over-heavy-lifting advice for a young athlete, though the speaker's advice is about a 13-year-old.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one simulated-game study, sample size not stated, no numbers shown for stress or velocity, and the mechanism is a hypothesis. It was pitchers in a simulated game, not a competition. Do not conclude that stress rises with fatigue in other sports or movements. Do not use the kinetic-chain idea to prescribe training; the speaker says he is only starting to study it.

**Example** — The speaker's own: velocity dips at inning five, yet stress rises instead of falling, unlike non-fatigued pitchers (z_6M5r7031A [05:40]).

**Related** — [[claim--faster-pitches-load-the-elbow-more]] (the relationship that broke down).

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally (sports medicine orthopedic surgeon and Detroit Lions team physician, per the host, z_6M5r7031A [00:00]) reports public-data cohort results on ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) reconstruction, "Tommy John surgery," in Major League Baseball pitchers. === claim--youth-specialization-survey-and-early-surgery
confidence: supported
# Year-Round Youth Baseball: Arm Pain Is Common, Pressure to Play On Is Common

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally gives early single-sport specialization and year-round play as the second reason UCL surgeries are not falling (z_6M5r7031A [06:10] to [07:10]). He says specialization before kids are skeletally mature is "causing a burnout" of muscles and tendons (z_6M5r7031A [07:10]).

- **Survey:** 200 healthy youth baseball players who were not complaining of pain, surveyed "when I was in residency in New York City." 75% admitted arm pain (z_6M5r7031A [07:10]). 25% had symptoms suggestive of a legitimate overuse injury, and 50% felt pressured to play despite admitting arm pain, by coaches and parents (z_6M5r7031A [07:41]).
- **Draft:** a Mayo Clinic study by Chris Camp (caption spelling), which the speaker reports second-hand, found up to 10% of drafted pitchers, high school and college, had already had Tommy John surgery, at an increasing rate year by year (z_6M5r7031A [07:41] to [08:11]).
- **Youngest case:** the youngest he has operated on was 12 (z_6M5r7031A [08:11]).
- **Qualifier (Q&A):** some early throwing is necessary because the arm remodels in childhood, including the humerus, so a child who never threw cannot take up pitching at 12; "the challenge is giving some rest" (z_6M5r7031A [19:51] to [20:21]). Pitch counts are undermined when school and travel leagues each count separately, and 15 warm-up pitches between innings add to a 70-pitch count (z_6M5r7031A [20:21]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's stated cause is no rest for the shoulder and elbow muscles across fall, winter, spring, summer, travel and high school ball (z_6M5r7031A [06:40]). The survey shows prevalence of pain and perceived pressure; it does not by itself show that specialization caused the injuries. Inference: the survey is cross-sectional, so cause cannot be read from it.

**When to apply** — As an outside prompt when Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance take medical or injury history from incoming baseball or softball athletes. Inference: ask about prior surgery and year-round throwing history, since the draft figure suggests earlier overuse changes what a prospect brings. Eric's baseline: progressions in volume and intensity are kept smooth, and abrupt changes are treated as an injury-risk driver (Inferred, HHPR 5355 course team position, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: this talk extends that with a youth-sport mechanism, accumulated load with no rest, which the baseline does not cover.

**When NOT to apply** — The survey's sample source, selection method and ages are not given beyond "200 healthy youth baseball players" in one residency setting. Self-reported pain is not a diagnosis. The Mayo figure is "up to 10%" and second-hand. The talk does not show that specialization causes the burnout; that is the speaker's assertion. Baseball pitching only. Not evidence about college or football athletes.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Little League kids icing their elbows after games, and facilities in Michigan full of children playing indoors in snow (z_6M5r7031A [06:10] to [07:10]).

**Related** — [[claim--faster-pitches-load-the-elbow-more]] (the first cause the speaker gives). [[claim--ucl-reconstruction-return-outcomes-mlb-pitchers]] (what happens after surgery).
=== framework--expected-value-decision-analysis-for-treatment-choice
confidence: untested
# Expected Value Decision Analysis for Surgery Versus Non-Operative Care

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally proposes expected value decision analysis as "an adjunct to our clinical care" for a UCL injury, after saying his group has used it in other parts of orthopedic surgery (z_6M5r7031A [15:46], [17:49]). The structure he describes:
1. **Two branches:** surgery, or non-operative treatment (the "top wing" and "bottom wing," z_6M5r7031A [16:16] to [16:47]).
2. **One outcome to maximize:** pitcher wins above replacement (WAR) in his example (z_6M5r7031A [16:47]).
3. **Inputs, known and unknown:** the likelihood of healing with and without surgery, the likely performance on return, and when the injury happened (z_6M5r7031A [15:46] to [16:16]). Context changes the answer: spring training versus a few months before the playoffs, and an ace on a team with no playoff chance versus a team on the bubble (z_6M5r7031A [16:16]).
4. **Output:** an expected value per branch. In his sample model, one representative scenario, expected WAR was 1.6 non-operative versus 1.3 with surgery (z_6M5r7031A [16:47]).
5. **Two-way sensitivity analysis:** a grid where blue tiles show surgery producing a better WAR and green tiles show non-operative care doing so, with threshold values for success by treatment based on clinical characteristics, prior attempts and tear characteristics. It lets the user toggle unknown inputs (z_6M5r7031A [17:19] to [17:49]).

Inputs he cites elsewhere: non-operative success of 40 to 80% depending on the case with at most a 3-month downtime, and surgery success of "80 to 100%" in different studies (caption "80 to 80 to 100%," garbled) with a year to a year and a half of downtime (z_6M5r7031A [14:14] to [14:45]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no argument beyond saying the model lets you "optimize for any outcome you want" and test unknown inputs (z_6M5r7031A [16:16], [17:49]). Inference: its value is making the assumptions explicit and showing where a decision flips, not producing a verdict.

**When to apply** — As an illustration when explaining a try-conservative-care versus choose-surgery conversation to coaches. Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's stated role is to supply information that supports Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine decisions (Explicit, Playbook p.6), and what it contributes in return to performance is testing and progression with shared loading decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4). Eric's baseline: "We don't assess readiness. The template answers that" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q22). Inference: a decision tree is a communication aid within that supporting role, and the probabilities in it belong to Athletic Medicine.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the only output shown is one sample case with chosen inputs, and no validation of the model against outcomes is shown. The speaker says it "does not take the place of clinical decision-making" (z_6M5r7031A [16:47]). The objective, WAR, is a professional baseball value measure with no college equivalent. The probabilities of healing are ranges from "different studies," not Baylor data. Do not use it to pick treatment for an athlete.

**Example** — The speaker's own sample: for one representative player, expected WAR of 1.6 with non-operative care versus 1.3 with surgery, so "maybe non-operative treatment might work" for this case (z_6M5r7031A [16:47]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--price-the-failure-branch-of-conservative-care]] (the logic of why the non-operative branch needs a failure term). [[claim--ucl-reconstruction-return-outcomes-mlb-pitchers]] (data that would fill the surgery branch). Reciprocal-link suggestions: [[yung-2022-a-framework-for-clinicians-to-improve-the-decision-making-process-in-return-to-sport]] (not compared in this batch) and [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].
=== heuristic--price-the-failure-branch-of-conservative-care
confidence: untested
# Before Trying Conservative Care First, Price What Happens If It Fails

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally answers the obvious proposal, "why not just let everybody try non-operative treatment" first, with a question: what if it does not work? (z_6M5r7031A [14:45] to [15:15]). If the trial burns 3 months of rest, activity modification and physical therapy and the athlete still needs surgery, then instead of losing one season by operating at once, "you've now lost two" (z_6M5r7031A [15:15]). His numbers for the two branches: non-operative success of 40 to 80% depending on the case, at most a 3-month downtime (z_6M5r7031A [14:14] to [14:45]); surgery downtime of a year to a year and a half, with a success rate the caption garbles as "80 to 80 to 100%" (z_6M5r7031A [14:45]). The follow-on question he poses: "How do we know who can benefit from surgery and who won't?" (z_6M5r7031A [15:15]), which he says is mostly clinical decision-making.

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the season count itself: a failed trial moves the operation later. Inference: because the cost is measured in lost seasons, the timing of the injury within the calendar matters, which fits his own point that spring training and the weeks before the playoffs are different injuries (z_6M5r7031A [16:16]).

**When to apply** — In any conversation where "try rehab first" is proposed for an injury that might still need surgery, to make the failure branch visible to coaches and athletes. Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine on return to performance and is not stated as the decision-maker (Explicit, Playbook p.6). Inference: the heuristic frames the question to ask Athletic Medicine; it does not answer it.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the success ranges are given without sources and the caption for the surgery range is garbled. The speaker's context is one UCL injury in professional pitchers, where a "season" is a fixed competitive calendar. The heuristic says nothing about injuries where conservative care is the standard first step. Not a basis for recommending surgery. The speaker says the choice is clinical.

**Example** — The speaker's own hypothetical: non-operative treatment tried first fails, and the player has "lost two" seasons instead of one (z_6M5r7031A [15:15]).

**Related** — [[framework--expected-value-decision-analysis-for-treatment-choice]] (the model that puts a number on the failure branch).

=== claim--mlb-surgery-counts-leveled-off-after-2014-with-no-causal-link
confidence: contested
# MLB Tommy John surgery counts spiked in 2012 to 2014, then leveled off, but the talk does not link that to the program and also says injuries are rising

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB league office) reports the trend from the public surgery database (caption "baseball heat mass", back to 1974) and from the league's electronic medical record (required of all clubs since 2010; the speaker says league data are not shared publicly until ready for peer review) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09], [01:39]).

The 2012 to 2014 spike (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:41], [03:12], [03:42], [04:12]):
- Disabled list days for the elbow injury were at an all-time high from 2012 to 2014, a 72% increase over the three years before (the injury is garbled in the caption as "Elvis trees").
- MLB surgeries: the previous high was 22; 36 in 2012; 31 in 2014.
- More of the players were 25 or younger than in any earlier five-year bucket, and many were top young pitchers; recovery is 12 to 16 months.
- The number having a second surgery rose steadily from 1995 to 2014.

The leveling off (sHXuxj3-rbQ [14:36], [15:06], [15:37]): roughly 20 to 25 players a year still have the procedure but "we didn't see the exponential growth" feared; the number of players drafted who had already had the surgery rose steadily to 2014, then was relatively flat over the last three years, though 2016 set an all-time high. In Q&A the speaker says the minor league record shows no linear upward trajectory, "goes up and down" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [25:22], [25:55]).

The speaker does not claim the program caused the leveling off.

Contradiction inside the talk, which the speaker does not reconcile: in the Q&A the speaker compares eras and says "the data kind of suggests ... that injuries are increasing" even though teams are more careful (sHXuxj3-rbQ [28:14], the captions are garbled around this sentence); that sits against the leveled-off statements at [14:36] to [15:37]. Another speaker in 2015 (Fleisig) said professional surgeries were still climbing and that youth and high school numbers had been "curved" (caption; read as curbed) a little but were still going up (AgouMNTeyo4 [07:42], [47:52]).

**Why it works** — Neither speaker gives a mechanism for the trend. Inference: a short window after a spike mixes a plateau with ordinary year-to-year noise; one or two years do not make a trend, as the speaker says in the Q&A ("tough to judge one or two-year trends", sHXuxj3-rbQ [25:22]).

**When to apply** — When a policy is credited for a leveling off in an injury count: check the window length, the denominator and whether the same data also say the opposite.

Eric's baseline: "When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19), and "We don't have any formal risk model that we follow." (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a count of cases without exposure (innings, pitches, athletes at risk) cannot support a causal story about a program.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `contested` because the talk both says the count leveled off and says injuries are increasing, and the 2015 talk describes a still-rising trend; the dates differ, so these may be consistent, but the 2017 Q&A is unclear. The leveling off rests on 2 to 3 years after a spike. There is no exposure denominator or comparison group, and 2016 itself was a record in the draftee count. The speaker works for the league office. Baseball only.

**Example** — The speaker's own: draftees with prior surgery rising to 2014 and then flat, with a 2016 record (sHXuxj3-rbQ [15:06], [15:37]).

**Related** — [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]]; [[claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree]] (2015 prevalence and return data); [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]].
=== claim--surgery-misperceptions-among-youth-players-and-parents
confidence: supported
# Players, parents and coaches overestimate what Tommy John surgery does

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB, director of league economics and strategy, sHXuxj3-rbQ [00:02], [00:37]) says a perception had grown that the surgery is always successful and returns a pitcher within a year throwing harder, and that players should have it before an injury to improve performance (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:41], [05:46]). A survey designed by a Yankees physician (caption "dr. mod"; the 2015 talk's caption "Dr Ahmad ... the New York Yankees doctor", probably the same survey, unconfirmed) went to youth players, coaches and parents asking how successful the surgery is, how long it takes, and whether the player will throw harder (sHXuxj3-rbQ [05:46]). Results as the speaker reports:
- More than half of high school players thought a player should have the surgery without an actual elbow injury.
- More than half of college players thought pitch speed increases afterward (sHXuxj3-rbQ [06:17]).

Fleisig's 2015 account of what appears to be the same survey gives different numbers: about two-thirds of respondents guessed about 60 percent make it back, about a third thought velocity goes up, a third to a half thought performance improves, and 25 to 50 percent thought surgery makes sense in some cases even without an injury, which the speaker calls "frightening" (AgouMNTeyo4 [18:30], [19:01], [19:33]). The speaker adds that pro teams sometimes tell the speaker a hurt pitcher should "just go get a surgery and get it over with", which is "not the right attitude", and that doctors say surgery is a last resort (AgouMNTeyo4 [18:00]). Fleisig's account also says the survey was run by a doctor and group at a New York clinic and the community, not the Yankees (AgouMNTeyo4 [18:30]). The two talks give different splits by group; do not harmonize them.

The speaker's response: the third part of the Pitch Smart program (see the program entry) gives accurate information so that players see surgery as "something I want to avoid, not something I want to have" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:55]).

**Why it works** — Neither speaker gives a mechanism for why the perception formed; DeAngelo lists it as one of the league's 2014 concerns (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:10]). Inference: when a rare success story (a star pitcher returning at full velocity) is visible and the outcome distribution is not, a perception gap forms, and measuring it is the first step in correcting it.

**When to apply** — As a method: before a recovery or rehab education effort, survey the athletes, coaches and parents on what they believe about outcomes, and compare to published outcomes. Also as a caution when staff or athletes describe a procedure as performance-enhancing.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's four operating principles include Research and Development and Performance Team Collaboration (Explicit, Playbook p.6), and in return to performance it contributes "Testing and progression", with shared loading decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4). The baseline holds no education survey of athletes' beliefs.

**When NOT to apply** — Baseball pitchers' beliefs about one surgery; the survey sample sizes, response rates and wording are not shown in either talk. The speaker says "all of our research and all the research of the medical community" shows the beliefs are incorrect, but Fleisig reports that one of three studies found performance improved after surgery (AgouMNTeyo4 [21:05], [21:39]), so "incorrect" on performance is contested (see the return-rate entry). The speaker is a league-office official describing the league's program. Do not use belief percentages from one talk as a Baylor estimate.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the survey result that more than half of high school players thought surgery without injury was reasonable (sHXuxj3-rbQ [05:46], [06:17]).

**Related** — [[claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree]] (2015 talk: what the outcome studies show); [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]].
=== framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft
confidence: untested
# A prospective cohort: baseline tests at entry, then follow every athlete through the medical record

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) describes the league's most significant research project with the players association: when a player is drafted he is asked for a baseline set (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:08]):
- A shoulder and elbow MRI.
- A full biomechanical evaluation.
- A playing-history questionnaire.

Each player is then followed for the rest of his career for performance, usage and future injuries, to see whether any baseline test or later behavior predicts injury, which can then inform preventive programs (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:39]). The design depends on the league's electronic medical record: since 2010 all clubs must use it, so the league does not need to keep going back to players to ask whether they were injured, which he says eliminates any participation or dropout rate (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09], [16:39]). So far 225 players are enrolled, with about 400 expected when baseline collection finishes (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:11]). The research partners are the players association, club medical staff and an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins; data are not shared publicly until ready for peer review (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09]).

The committee's research questions, listed separately from this study (the speaker does not tie them to it) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [10:25], [11:26], [11:57], [12:30]): at the professional level, whether biomechanics, usage or velocity matter as risk factors; whether the rehab process or future usage can reduce second surgeries; whether surgical variants (graft, technique) affect success; and whether alternative therapies can shorten the 12 to 16 month rehab or avoid surgery.

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is that the record removes loss to follow-up, one of the main weaknesses of long cohort studies (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:39]). Inference: baseline data recorded before any injury is what lets a later injury be compared to something measured earlier; the 2015 spring-training study could not do this because it met pitchers only after they had returned (AgouMNTeyo4 [29:22]).

**When to apply** — When deciding what to record at entry for each athlete so that later injuries can be studied: a short history of prior workload and injury, the physical baselines already collected, and a way to link them to later records.

Eric's baseline: each source system holds its own data and the source wins over the aggregating platform (Kitman) when they disagree (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q11); there is no common testing cadence across sports (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q9); no formal injury-risk model is in use (Explicit, Q12). Data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Inference: a Baylor version would be a small intake record linked to existing VALD and GPS data, not an MRI program, and its value depends on the consistency of collection that Eric's NordBord decision stressed.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the talk reports design and enrollment only, with no results. The data are not public, so the claims cannot be checked. It rests on a league-wide record system that every club must use (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09]); Baylor's follow-up would depend on its own record system and on a stable staff. Teams also guard training data as a competitive advantage, so the league works with a select group of teams on granular training data (sHXuxj3-rbQ [28:44]). Professional draftees, not college athletes. The speaker works for the league office. Do not add collection until a question exists.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 225-player enrollment, with follow-up by the medical record rather than by contacting players (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:39], [17:11]).

**Related** — [[case-study--spring-training-field-lab-post-surgery-vs-never-injured]] (2015 talk: a post-hoc comparison with no pre-injury data); [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]]; [[principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance]].
=== claim--partial-ucl-tear-rest-study-43-players
confidence: untested
# Rest alone for partial UCL tears: 93% of 43 players returned without surgery, and tear location may predict who fails

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) describes two team-physician studies of the league's own players, in the area of conservative care and rehab where he sees "very promising studies" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:42], [18:13]):
- The Colorado Rockies' study of players with partial UCL tears, in the middle ground between a full tear that means surgery and an injury that might not need it: after six to eight weeks of rest, 93% came back and pitched without surgery (caption: "pitched with that name surgery", read as without surgery). The sample was 43 players, and the speaker says "it's tough to really draw too many conclusions from that" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [18:13], [18:43]). 93% of 43 is about 40 players (Inference, my arithmetic).
- A similar study by a Cleveland Indians physician (name garbled in the captions) asked whether the location of the tear predicts who returns: players with distal tears were "much more likely to fail the rehab" and need surgery than players with proximal tears (sHXuxj3-rbQ [18:43], [19:14]).

His takeaway: the medical community is getting "more strategic and accurate" about which injuries lend themselves to conservative care and which "you probably should just opt for the surgery and kind of come back more quickly" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [19:14]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism. Inference: a partial tear can heal or fail, and tear location sorts the two groups; the studies as reported do not show how, and the rest window is the same 6 to 8 weeks that the orthobiologic users also wait (see the evidence-lag entry).

**When to apply** — As a reason to ask Athletic Medicine whether a defined rest window before testing is reasonable for a partial injury, and what Applied Performance testing would show at the end of it. This is a question for Athletic Medicine, not a recommendation.

=== principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance
confidence: untested
# Throwing harder both raises injury risk and improves performance, so the goal is balance

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) answers a Q&A question on velocity: a lot of the evidence suggests that throwing harder increases the risk of injury, and there is "also a lot of evidence" that throwing harder improves performance, so a player is more likely to reach higher levels (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23]; the caption is garbled in places). It is tough, he says, to tell someone not to throw as hard, because velocity may be essential to performing. His position: do not focus on throwing hard "to the exclusion of" mechanics and locating the ball; find a balance among them (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23], [30:53]). He also says three recent studies pointed to greater fastball usage, throwing harder, pitching more in individual games and resting less as associated with UCL injury risk, and calls the field "very preliminary" and dependent on public data (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:11], [17:42]). In the same Q&A he says throwing is a stressful task and injuries can be reduced but "never" eradicated (sHXuxj3-rbQ [29:22], [29:52]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and cites neither the evidence on risk nor the evidence on performance. Fleisig's 2015 talk offers a related point: poor mechanics raise arm stress and cost velocity, and good mechanics give more velocity and less stress, though the step from arm stress to injury is unproven (AgouMNTeyo4 [24:45], [58:38]). Inference: if both hold, mechanics is the lever that can improve the trade, which is what "balance" asks for.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's development plan treats a single outcome number (velocity, jump height, top speed) as the target: ask what else rises with it, and track the cost alongside the gain.

Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, density and training means, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position). Speed is described as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: the two baseline positions meet in this entry's tension, and the baseline does not say how Baylor resolves it for football.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an expert's general statement in a Q&A; neither the injury evidence nor the performance evidence is named, and the three risk-factor studies are "very preliminary" by his own description. It is pitching velocity in baseball, from a league-office official. Do not use it to justify limiting any athlete's speed or velocity development, or to infer a football speed-injury relationship. The 2015 speaker (Fleisig) says average fastball velocity rose by about 2 mph since 2002, from a news clip shown in his talk, not from his data (AgouMNTeyo4 [10:15]).

**Example** — The speaker's own framing: the player who throws harder is likelier to reach higher levels yet may carry more injury risk (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23]).

**Related** — [[claim--curveballs-not-shown-more-stressful-than-fastballs]] (2015 talk: pitch type and elbow torque); [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]]; [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]].
=== framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program
confidence: untested
# Pitch Smart: a three-part program of count limits, plain-language research and accurate surgery information

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) describes how the league office turned a medical committee's research into a youth program. In 2014 the Commissioner's Office convened leading medical experts (the speaker names Dr Andrews and a research director whose name and institution are garbled in the caption: "dr. fly cigs who's dr. introduces research director", plus team physicians and researchers) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [06:52]). They told it that the single greatest factor was youth overuse and rest, and that "very modifiable" behaviors correlated with injury in youth; the best study followed youth pitchers for ten years and found 100 or more innings a year went with more serious arm injury (sHXuxj3-rbQ [07:22], [07:54]). GMs, coaches and players also said specializing early and playing year round with high single-game pitch counts raised risk (sHXuxj3-rbQ [08:24]).

The program, with USA Baseball, launched in November 2014 (caption "pitch mark", "pitch smart", read here as Pitch Smart) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [08:54], [12:30]). Three parts (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24], [09:55]):
- Pitch count limits and required rest guidelines from age 7 to 22, with allowed pitches rising by age and rest days rising with pitches thrown in a game; example: throw 50 pitches, wait two days before pitching again (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24], [10:25]).
- Research synthesized into digestible information for players and coaches, so they understand why.
- Accurate information about Tommy John surgery.

Adoption (sHXuxj3-rbQ [13:03], [13:33], [14:04], [14:36]): Little League already had guidelines; showcase circuits (caption "perfect game") and college summer leagues including the Cape Cod League comply; in 2014 Vermont was the only state with a pitch-count-based high school rule; in 2016 the National Federation of State High School Associations voted to require states to adopt a pitch-count and required-rest rule; in 2017 the speaker counts 44 or 46 states (the caption is ambiguous) with Connecticut and Massachusetts as holdouts. States do not all follow the Pitch Smart table exactly.

**Why it works** — The speaker's logic is that the research already existed and the rest-after-a-count rule (the 50 pitches, two days example) is "a pretty intuitive concept" that had not been widely adopted (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24]). The speaker gives no evidence that adoption reduced injuries. Inference: the program's contribution is distribution and compliance, not new evidence, which is how an overuse rule becomes a rule.

**When to apply** — As a model for converting a research finding into an enforceable exposure rule: name an authority, set limits that scale by age and dose, publish the reasons, and recruit governing bodies. Inference: for Baylor, the equivalent is a written exposure rule a staff member can apply the same way each time.

Eric's baseline: smooth, gradual progression is treated as protective and abrupt changes as an injury-risk driver (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position); in-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (Inferred, transcript and shared slides, not claimed in interview). The baseline holds no throwing or contact-exposure rule. Inference: a pitch count with rest is a dose rule of that kind.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `untested` because the talk shows no outcome for the program: the speaker said surgeries leveled off and did not claim the guidelines caused it (sHXuxj3-rbQ [14:36], [15:37]). The speaker works for the league office and describes the league's own program. The age and pitch table is not reproduced in the transcript, so no specific limit can be cited from this talk. Youth baseball pitchers; do not transfer to football. The 2012 concussion speaker, discussing pitch counts, calls the age caps "clearly not based on much science" (npgdKKdJSww [17:19]), a caution on how much weight a count table can bear.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 2016 high school federation vote, from one state with a rule to nearly all (sHXuxj3-rbQ [13:33], [14:04], [14:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]] (the 2015 talk's cohort result behind the guideline); [[claim--mlb-surgery-counts-leveled-off-after-2014-with-no-causal-link]]; [[framework--hit-count-as-exposure-budget-modeled-on-pitch-count]]; [[claim--surgery-misperceptions-among-youth-players-and-parents]].
=== principle--recovery-and-training-methods-run-ahead-of-evidence
confidence: untested
# New recovery and training methods spread faster than the evidence for them

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) says "research sometimes lags behind what the medical community moves toward", and gives three examples (sHXuxj3-rbQ [19:44], [20:14]):
- Orthobiologics (PRP, stem cells): increasingly popular, but there have not been many peer-reviewed articles showing they work better than rest and rehab alone (sHXuxj3-rbQ [20:14]). One Los Angeles surgeon (caption "dr. Yoon") reports anecdotally better results with stem cells than PRP; another (caption "dr. Ella trash", likely ElAttrache) makes the same confounding point: patients wait three, four, six or eight weeks, so "is it the rest or is it the ortho biologic?" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [20:44], [21:16]). Of the MLB pitchers who used them in 2016 (from "baseball heat maps records", per the caption): one came back successfully (caption name "Michael Lorenzen"), three had already had surgery, and four were still waiting (sHXuxj3-rbQ [21:16], [21:47]).
- Club technology and training methods: clubs want an edge and use devices to track fatigue, injury risk and stress variables; a Seattle outfit (caption "drivelines") with "unorthodox training methods" has become popular among some teams, and "it's tough to tell whether this actually helps" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [22:18], [22:49], [23:19]). A team that succeeds in one area is copied by others (sHXuxj3-rbQ [23:19]).
- A repair technique: Dr Dugas (caption "dugas @andrew sports medicine") repairs the UCL with tape augmentation, with an expected recovery of about six months instead of 12 to 16 (the caption reads "six to six months post 12 to 16", garbled); experimental, for certain tears only, with early positive results in high school and college players and two Cardinals pitchers expected back for spring training (sHXuxj3-rbQ [23:52], [24:22]). The speaker says the medical community approaches it "with skepticism" awaiting research.

His summary: there is "still a lot to learn about this area", and it is difficult to make sweeping statements from the data available now (sHXuxj3-rbQ [21:47]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is competitive pressure and imitation (sHXuxj3-rbQ [22:18], [23:19]). Inference: when each recovery involves a waiting period, any treatment applied at the start of the wait is confounded with rest unless a comparison arm exists.

**When to apply** — Before adopting a new recovery, rehab or monitoring technology: ask for a comparison against rest or the current protocol, and for what happens to everyone who tried it, not the successes.

Eric's baseline: a test or technology that does not answer a question someone has "doesn't have a place" (interview 2026-09-28, Q3, Explicit); NordBord testing was retired for roster-wide use because it could not be run consistently, and kept only for small groups with a clear clinical purpose and dedicated oversight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-20); data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Recovery at Baylor is managed through load design with nothing objective tracked (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q23). Inference: the standard Eric applies to testing technology is the one DeAngelo suggests applying to recovery technology.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the speaker's claim is a general observation with a handful of examples (eight pitchers, two surgeons' opinions) and no systematic review. The speaker is a league-office official (Inference: not a clinician) and describes one surgeon's results as anecdotal; the other surgeon's point is the rest confound. It is not evidence that the methods do not work; the point is that the evidence is not there yet. Do not use it to dismiss a technology without a trial of your own.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 2016 list of MLB pitchers who used PRP or stem cells (one successful, three had surgery, four waiting) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [21:16], [21:47]).

**Related** — [[claim--partial-ucl-tear-rest-study-43-players]] (the rest comparison the orthobiologic question needs); [[krystofiak-2024-injection-of-amniotic-membrane-and-umbilical-cord-particulate-for-muscle-and-ligament-tear]] (a paper note on injections for tendon and ligament tears); [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] (Old Bull).

# Throwing harder both raises injury risk and improves performance, so the goal is balance

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) answers a Q&A question on velocity: a lot of the evidence suggests that throwing harder increases the risk of injury, and there is "also a lot of evidence" that throwing harder improves performance, so a player is more likely to reach higher levels (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23]; the caption is garbled in places). It is tough, he says, to tell someone not to throw as hard, because velocity may be essential to performing. His position: do not focus on throwing hard "to the exclusion of" mechanics and locating the ball; find a balance among them (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23], [30:53]). He also says three recent studies pointed to greater fastball usage, throwing harder, pitching more in individual games and resting less as associated with UCL injury risk, and calls the field "very preliminary" and dependent on public data (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:11], [17:42]). In the same Q&A he says throwing is a stressful task and injuries can be reduced but "never" eradicated (sHXuxj3-rbQ [29:22], [29:52]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and cites neither the evidence on risk nor the evidence on performance. Fleisig's 2015 talk offers a related point: poor mechanics raise arm stress and cost velocity, and good mechanics give more velocity and less stress, though the step from arm stress to injury is unproven (AgouMNTeyo4 [24:45], [58:38]). Inference: if both hold, mechanics is the lever that can improve the trade, which is what "balance" asks for.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's development plan treats a single outcome number (velocity, jump height, top speed) as the target: ask what else rises with it, and track the cost alongside the gain.

Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, density and training means, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position). Speed is described as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: the two baseline positions meet in this entry's tension, and the baseline does not say how Baylor resolves it for football.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an expert's general statement in a Q&A; neither the injury evidence nor the performance evidence is named, and the three risk-factor studies are "very preliminary" by his own description. It is pitching velocity in baseball, from a league-office official. Do not use it to justify limiting any athlete's speed or velocity development, or to infer a football speed-injury relationship. The 2015 speaker (Fleisig) says average fastball velocity rose by about 2 mph since 2002, from a news clip shown in his talk, not from his data (AgouMNTeyo4 [10:15]).

**Example** — The speaker's own framing: the player who throws harder is likelier to reach higher levels yet may carry more injury risk (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23]).

**Related** — [[claim--curveballs-not-shown-more-stressful-than-fastballs]] (2015 talk: pitch type and elbow torque); [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]]; [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]].
