# Pitch Smart: a three-part program of count limits, plain-language research and accurate surgery information

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) describes how the league office turned a medical committee's research into a youth program. In 2014 the Commissioner's Office convened leading medical experts (the speaker names Dr Andrews and a research director whose name and institution are garbled in the caption: "dr. fly cigs who's dr. introduces research director", plus team physicians and researchers) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [06:52]). They told it that the single greatest factor was youth overuse and rest, and that "very modifiable" behaviors correlated with injury in youth; the best study followed youth pitchers for ten years and found 100 or more innings a year went with more serious arm injury (sHXuxj3-rbQ [07:22], [07:54]). GMs, coaches and players also said specializing early and playing year round with high single-game pitch counts raised risk (sHXuxj3-rbQ [08:24]).

The program, with USA Baseball, launched in November 2014 (caption "pitch mark", "pitch smart", read here as Pitch Smart) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [08:54], [12:30]). Three parts (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24], [09:55]):
- Pitch count limits and required rest guidelines from age 7 to 22, with allowed pitches rising by age and rest days rising with pitches thrown in a game; example: throw 50 pitches, wait two days before pitching again (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24], [10:25]).
- Research synthesized into digestible information for players and coaches, so they understand why.
- Accurate information about Tommy John surgery.

Adoption (sHXuxj3-rbQ [13:03], [13:33], [14:04], [14:36]): Little League already had guidelines; showcase circuits (caption "perfect game") and college summer leagues including the Cape Cod League comply; in 2014 Vermont was the only state with a pitch-count-based high school rule; in 2016 the National Federation of State High School Associations voted to require states to adopt a pitch-count and required-rest rule; in 2017 the speaker counts 44 or 46 states (the caption is ambiguous) with Connecticut and Massachusetts as holdouts. States do not all follow the Pitch Smart table exactly.

**Why it works** — The speaker's logic is that the research already existed and the rest-after-a-count rule (the 50 pitches, two days example) is "a pretty intuitive concept" that had not been widely adopted (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24]). The speaker gives no evidence that adoption reduced injuries. Inference: the program's contribution is distribution and compliance, not new evidence, which is how an overuse rule becomes a rule.

**When to apply** — As a model for converting a research finding into an enforceable exposure rule: name an authority, set limits that scale by age and dose, publish the reasons, and recruit governing bodies. Inference: for Baylor, the equivalent is a written exposure rule a staff member can apply the same way each time.

Eric's baseline: smooth, gradual progression is treated as protective and abrupt changes as an injury-risk driver (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position); in-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (Inferred, transcript and shared slides, not claimed in interview). The baseline holds no throwing or contact-exposure rule. Inference: a pitch count with rest is a dose rule of that kind.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `untested` because the talk shows no outcome for the program: the speaker said surgeries leveled off and did not claim the guidelines caused it (sHXuxj3-rbQ [14:36], [15:37]). The speaker works for the league office and describes the league's own program. The age and pitch table is not reproduced in the transcript, so no specific limit can be cited from this talk. Youth baseball pitchers; do not transfer to football. The 2012 concussion speaker, discussing pitch counts, calls the age caps "clearly not based on much science" (npgdKKdJSww [17:19]), a caution on how much weight a count table can bear.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 2016 high school federation vote, from one state with a rule to nearly all (sHXuxj3-rbQ [13:33], [14:04], [14:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]] (the 2015 talk's cohort result behind the guideline); [[claim--mlb-surgery-counts-leveled-off-after-2014-with-no-causal-link]]; [[framework--hit-count-as-exposure-budget-modeled-on-pitch-count]]; [[claim--surgery-misperceptions-among-youth-players-and-parents]].

# New recovery and training methods spread faster than the evidence for them

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) says "research sometimes lags behind what the medical community moves toward", and gives three examples (sHXuxj3-rbQ [19:44], [20:14]):
- Orthobiologics (PRP, stem cells): increasingly popular, but there have not been many peer-reviewed articles showing they work better than rest and rehab alone (sHXuxj3-rbQ [20:14]). One Los Angeles surgeon (caption "dr. Yoon") reports anecdotally better results with stem cells than PRP; another (caption "dr. Ella trash", likely ElAttrache) makes the same confounding point: patients wait three, four, six or eight weeks, so "is it the rest or is it the ortho biologic?" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [20:44], [21:16]). Of the MLB pitchers who used them in 2016 (from "baseball heat maps records", per the caption): one came back successfully (caption name "Michael Lorenzen"), three had already had surgery, and four were still waiting (sHXuxj3-rbQ [21:16], [21:47]).
- Club technology and training methods: clubs want an edge and use devices to track fatigue, injury risk and stress variables; a Seattle outfit (caption "drivelines") with "unorthodox training methods" has become popular among some teams, and "it's tough to tell whether this actually helps" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [22:18], [22:49], [23:19]). A team that succeeds in one area is copied by others (sHXuxj3-rbQ [23:19]).
- A repair technique: Dr Dugas (caption "dugas @andrew sports medicine") repairs the UCL with tape augmentation, with an expected recovery of about six months instead of 12 to 16 (the caption reads "six to six months post 12 to 16", garbled); experimental, for certain tears only, with early positive results in high school and college players and two Cardinals pitchers expected back for spring training (sHXuxj3-rbQ [23:52], [24:22]). The speaker says the medical community approaches it "with skepticism" awaiting research.

His summary: there is "still a lot to learn about this area", and it is difficult to make sweeping statements from the data available now (sHXuxj3-rbQ [21:47]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is competitive pressure and imitation (sHXuxj3-rbQ [22:18], [23:19]). Inference: when each recovery involves a waiting period, any treatment applied at the start of the wait is confounded with rest unless a comparison arm exists.

**When to apply** — Before adopting a new recovery, rehab or monitoring technology: ask for a comparison against rest or the current protocol, and for what happens to everyone who tried it, not the successes.

Eric's baseline: a test or technology that does not answer a question someone has "doesn't have a place" (interview 2026-09-28, Q3, Explicit); NordBord testing was retired for roster-wide use because it could not be run consistently, and kept only for small groups with a clear clinical purpose and dedicated oversight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-20); data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Recovery at Baylor is managed through load design with nothing objective tracked (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q23). Inference: the standard Eric applies to testing technology is the one DeAngelo suggests applying to recovery technology.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the speaker's claim is a general observation with a handful of examples (eight pitchers, two surgeons' opinions) and no systematic review. The speaker is a league-office official (Inference: not a clinician) and describes one surgeon's results as anecdotal; the other surgeon's point is the rest confound. It is not evidence that the methods do not work; the point is that the evidence is not there yet. Do not use it to dismiss a technology without a trial of your own.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 2016 list of MLB pitchers who used PRP or stem cells (one successful, three had surgery, four waiting) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [21:16], [21:47]).

**Related** — [[claim--partial-ucl-tear-rest-study-43-players]] (the rest comparison the orthobiologic question needs); [[krystofiak-2024-injection-of-amniotic-membrane-and-umbilical-cord-particulate-for-muscle-and-ligament-tear]] (a paper note on injections for tendon and ligament tears); [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] (Old Bull).

lines: # Defining "proper mechanics" as the mean and spread of healthy, high-velocity pitchers

-**What it is** — Asked how he knows what proper mechanics are, Glenn Fleisig describes his criteria: the pitcher came to his lab, had not been injured for at least a year, and had a high fastball velocity during the test (AgouMNTeyo4 [54:32], [55:03]). He took about 150 such pitchers (by his account including Roger Clemens, and "some college guy you never heard of"), computed the mean and standard deviation of each measurement (stride length is his example), and calls that range proper mechanics: in effect the 150 best pitchers he has tested by ball velocity (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:03], [55:33]; the caption says "pictures", read here as pitchers). Studies then showed pitchers outside those ranges, as a group, had lower ball velocity and higher stress on the arm (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:33], [56:03]). He has also tested over 2,000 pitchers in the lab, including eight who went on to win Cy Young awards (caption "sa young", "15 sa young Awards"), with 12 cameras and about 40 markers (AgouMNTeyo4 [13:20], [13:51], [43:13]).

+**What it is** — Asked how he knows what proper mechanics are, Glenn Fleisig describes his criteria: the pitcher came to his lab, had not been injured for at least a year, and had a high fastball velocity during the test (AgouMNTeyo4 [54:32], [55:03]). He took about 150 such pitchers (by his account including Roger Clemens, and "some college guy you never heard of"), computed the mean and standard deviation of each measurement (stride length is his example), and calls that range proper mechanics: in effect the 150 best pitchers he has tested by ball velocity (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:03], [55:33]; the caption says "pictures", read here as pitchers). Studies then showed pitchers outside those ranges, as a group, had lower ball velocity and higher stress on the arm (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:33], [56:03]). He has also tested over 2,000 pitchers in the lab, including eight who went on to win Cy Young awards (caption "sa young", "15 sa young Awards") (AgouMNTeyo4 [13:20], [13:51]). A promotional video shown in the talk, whose narrator the captions do not identify, describes the setup as 12 cameras tracking about 40 markers (AgouMNTeyo4 [43:13]).

His own account of the limits: when asked whether pitchers measured with poor mechanics later got hurt, "it was a mixed bag", about half did and half did not. He says mechanics is only one factor, that his lab intervenes by telling pitchers what they do wrong (so some may fix it), and that the step from higher arm stress to more injury is "a leap of faith" that he has not proven (AgouMNTeyo4 [58:06], [58:38]).

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

# MLB Tommy John surgery counts spiked in 2012 to 2014, then leveled off, but the talk does not link that to the program and also says injuries are rising

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB league office) reports the trend from the public surgery database (caption "baseball heat mass", back to 1974) and from the league's electronic medical record (required of all clubs since 2010; the speaker says league data are not shared publicly until ready for peer review) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09], [01:39]).

The 2012 to 2014 spike (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:41], [03:12], [03:42], [04:12]):
- Disabled list days for the elbow injury were at an all-time high from 2012 to 2014, a 72% increase over the three years before (the injury is garbled in the caption as "Elvis trees").
- MLB surgeries: the previous high was 22; 36 in 2012; 31 in 2014.
- More of the players were 25 or younger than in any earlier five-year bucket, and many were top young pitchers; recovery is 12 to 16 months.
- The number having a second surgery rose steadily from 1995 to 2014.

The leveling off (sHXuxj3-rbQ [14:36], [15:06], [15:37]): roughly 20 to 25 players a year still have the procedure but "we didn't see the exponential growth" feared; the number of players drafted who had already had the surgery rose steadily to 2014, then was relatively flat over the last three years, though 2016 set an all-time high. In Q&A the speaker says the minor league record shows no linear upward trajectory, "goes up and down" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [25:22], [25:55]).

The speaker does not claim the program caused the leveling off.

Contradiction inside the talk, which the speaker does not reconcile: in the Q&A the speaker compares eras and says "the data kind of suggests ... that injuries are increasing" even though teams are more careful (sHXuxj3-rbQ [28:14], the captions are garbled around this sentence); that sits against the leveled-off statements at [14:36] to [15:37]. Another speaker in 2015 (Fleisig) said professional surgeries were still climbing and that youth and high school numbers had been "curved" (caption; read as curbed) a little but were still going up (AgouMNTeyo4 [07:42], [47:52]).

**Why it works** — Neither speaker gives a mechanism for the trend. Inference: a short window after a spike mixes a plateau with ordinary year-to-year noise; one or two years do not make a trend, as the speaker says in the Q&A ("tough to judge one or two-year trends", sHXuxj3-rbQ [25:22]).

**When to apply** — When a policy is credited for a leveling off in an injury count: check the window length, the denominator and whether the same data also say the opposite.

Eric's baseline: "When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19), and "We don't have any formal risk model that we follow." (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a count of cases without exposure (innings, pitches, athletes at risk) cannot support a causal story about a program.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `contested` because the talk both says the count leveled off and says injuries are increasing, and the 2015 talk describes a still-rising trend; the dates differ, so these may be consistent, but the 2017 Q&A is unclear. The leveling off rests on 2 to 3 years after a spike. There is no exposure denominator or comparison group, and 2016 itself was a record in the draftee count. The speaker works for the league office. Baseball only.

**Example** — The speaker's own: draftees with prior surgery rising to 2014 and then flat, with a 2016 record (sHXuxj3-rbQ [15:06], [15:37]).

**Related** — [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]]; [[claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree]] (2015 prevalence and return data); [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]].
